documents.title: The Joy of Non-Recognition
paragraphs: I do not understand such a phenomenon as 'the audience as a whole'. The idea of the audience as a single organism directed toward one point or another no longer seems to work. Art has become stratified, and the audience along with it. Every direction — and there are infinitely many now, as many directions as authors, as many styles as composers — finds its own audience. The very concept of a large audience is disappearing. Familiar things continue to work by inertia for the majority, while many parallel processes simultaneously gather their own surprisingly diverse and extensive audiences.

For a long time society had a strong tradition of uniting around an artwork that was supposed to be understandable to the majority. Today this mechanism no longer works. Not because there are no worthy authors capable of creating works that could unite millions, but because art now separates. And by separating, it emphasizes the uniqueness, irreducibility, and value of each element. Contemporary art treats each individual listener with greater trust than art that conceives of the listener as a mass.

I do not want to perceive my audience as a mass. It is very important to me that people who come into the hall experience themselves as unique units, see that different processes are taking place in themselves and in the person sitting beside them, and respect that difference. To propose a situation in which the listener perceives both themselves and their neighbor as separate and valuable in themselves is a major task.

Contemporary art does not flirt with familiar models that provoke an unambiguous emotional response: this is funny, this is cheerful, this is sad. It creates abstract situations that provoke different reactions in every listener. Personally, I do not want to feel like everyone else; I want to feel in my own unique way, and I want the person I love to feel in their own way too, rather than like several million other people. Bringing out this difference of feeling is very important, although it can be quite painful.

There is an element of public exposure in what I am writing now, the discomfort of finding oneself in the situation: 'I am different, everyone is looking at me.' This is what the aggressive reaction to contemporary art is connected with. Not with art itself, but with the position in which it places the perceiver: 'I don't understand, therefore I'm an idiot. They are making an idiot of me.' But why does 'I don't understand' equal 'I'm an idiot'? Why is not understanding something negative?

Understanding and misunderstanding can be programmed by the author. There are laws that make an artwork understandable. Misunderstanding, however, is an unexplored territory of perception that we often marginalize ourselves and try to eliminate. But perhaps this very territory can reveal in us a new type of feeling, a new type of relationship with ourselves and others. What is misunderstanding? Why do we feel discomfort but do not want to discover how to interact with it?

Everyone constructs their relationship with an artwork from zero, and all these relationships are unique. We need to listen to ourselves, to our inner reactions; we need to be surprised. Encountering misunderstanding, it is as if we fail to recognize ourselves, as if we cannot fit ourselves to the proposed situation. In everyday reality such a situation may conceal a danger to life. In art there is no such danger. Art functions as a training device developing the muscle that reacts to a situation of misunderstanding. Why should a person not explore this new territory and learn to inhabit it?

The territory of misunderstanding is infinite, while what is available to our understanding is extremely limited. Contemporary art's intrusion into this territory is the exploration of a new dimension. In some situations proposed by contemporary art, we move beyond familiar space and gain the possibility of seeing something there. We have not yet developed a conceptual apparatus capable of defining everything we see there, but that requires time.

A view from the territory of misunderstanding renews the realm of the understandable. We look at the familiar with different eyes. The difficulty lies at the starting point: are you ready to relinquish the negativity arising in an uncomfortable situation, turn it into something positive, and accept and respect the Other, understanding that you yourself are other in relation to this object, that you are equidistant points?

Every person is a separate world in which its own laws, harmony, hierarchy, and preferences operate. Every artwork is also a separate, complete world. One must be born and die within it. In some works this life is lived intensely; elsewhere it contains fewer events. But in any case we have the possibility of learning to orient ourselves within the space of the life taking place in the work. We all do this differently.

The process of perception resembles looking into darkness. As the eyes adapt to the dark, the outlines of objects filling the space begin to emerge, whether real or not. We endow these objects and phenomena with characteristics that allow what we see to fit into a system acceptable and convenient to us. Under such conditions, every perceiver constructs their world from zero, and these newly created worlds differ according to each person's individual features, experience, preferences, and expectations.

documents.title: Overcoming Music
paragraphs: An artwork is an act of violently endowing content with form. Violently, because by and large content has no need of form. Content exists before form and outside it. It is not comprehended; it is guessed at. Ultimately, the form of a work is a way of pointing toward what exists outside it. Forms are infinitely diverse; content is always one — probably the only content accessible to us: ourselves.

I do not want to lead the listener: now you will be cheerful, now a little sad, at the golden section you will experience catharsis, then a few minutes reflecting on what you have been through, and finally, enlightened and purified, you can go home and eat pasta. A cultural all-inclusive package. On the contrary, I want to give the listener a chance to be alone with themselves. For this, perception has to be detached from form, which distracts us from content and blocks it from view.

Music is one of these forms or machines of cognition. We stretch what we hear over our own preferences, expectations, stereotypes, and if it begins to pinch and chafe, we throw it away. There is generalized content before exemplification; meaning is exemplified content.

Forms are keyholes through which we peek at content. The shapes of these keyholes differ. But anyone who mistakes the content visible through them for the ultimate content is deeply mistaken. The more form obstructs exemplification, the greater the chance of sensing the proximity and fullness of content. Form is simultaneously a path toward content and an obstacle on that path. One can come closest to content only by attempting to dissolve within it. To do that, form must be overcome.

The history of the professional European musical tradition is a history of liberations and overcomings — of conventions, systems, schemes. One of the first was the liberation of sound from the dictate of the word. Music eventually detached itself from text. Literature made a corresponding movement through concrete poetry and textual objects; visual art began freeing itself from representation and eventually from the image itself.

The next stage in music can be described as a movement toward liberation from sound. Over time, pause and silence acquire increasing significance. Beginning with syntactic functions, silence fills with independent meanings: the silence of expectation, the silence of reflection, the silence of complete stoppage, stasis. Finally, Cage's sounding total silence. By exposing silence, Cage showed that it does not exist. Silence is what we agree to call silence. In a city, silence is the hum of traffic outside the window; in a forest, the rustling of leaves; by the sea, the sound of the surf. By setting out on the path of liberation from sound, music taught us to hear silence.

Sound is the tension of silence, its form. Silence is always very complexly organized; it contains many layers, perspectives, depths. Sound demands listening; silence demands listening into. Sound demands distinction and tracking; silence demands discernment and discovery. Silence changes the paradigm of listening attention: from the horizontal and vertical system of relationships between sounds, we move into depth, into the perspective of sound, receding from us and entering us at the same time.
Being part of silence, we become part of sound. In silence, sound acquires totality and omnipresence. Thus music becomes one of the paths toward a boundary beyond which it is no longer necessary.

documents.title: The Space of Sound. There's a Man Walking There
paragraphs: I am regularly asked how one can learn to listen to and understand contemporary music. Many people imagine it as a deeply marginal territory serving the interests of a narrow circle of initiates, a territory on which familiar instruments of perception do not work. But is that really so? When listening to Mozart or Lachenmann, are we dealing with different elements, different mechanisms of understanding? In the first case, models of perception developed and absorbed since childhood become active, and it seems to us that we understand, that we hear. In the second, those models do not switch on; on the contrary, the author seems deliberately to avoid allowing them to switch on. What are we to do?

Many years ago I was listening at home on headphones to Helmut Lachenmann's Kontrakadenz. My five-year-old son came over and asked what I was doing. I said: listening. After listening attentively for a while, he quietly asked: what is it? It is music, I answered. He listened a little longer and said: no, it isn't music... My heart sank — out of the mouths of babes... But he continued: there's a man walking there! And he listened with interest for another couple of minutes.

Before asking difficult questions about the nature of hearing, acoustics, psychoacoustics, structural or phenomenological analysis, perhaps one should discover in oneself a readiness to perceive something new in principle. Hearing is one of the instruments of self-knowledge. Are we ready to find ourselves inside new, incomprehensible, unfamiliar acoustic situations and try to establish communicative connections within them? If we are, then it does not matter whether it is Classical music, Romantic music, Expressionism, radical avant-garde, the sounds of factories or nature — everywhere we hear ourselves and deal with our readiness to understand and accept what is heard.

Every author, and sometimes every individual work, is a complete world, a small epoch existing simultaneously with many parallel epochs. Such a situation demands an entirely different intensity of listening than one in which long-assimilated rules and historically established models and conventions of perception, composition, and interpretation operate across relatively large communities for relatively long periods of historical time.

I often compare perceiving a musical work with visiting a museum. There are at least two ways to visit a museum: with a guide and without one. The guide leads the group along a predetermined route, drawing attention to particular exhibits and details. The guide acts as an author, constructing their own dramaturgy of the museum. But one can imagine another situation: a person walks through the museum alone. They can construct their own dramaturgy, their own trajectories. For someone it may become a museum of one painting; for someone else, a museum of windows or doors.

In the first case we deal with an authorial, external narrative — the author's intention to lead the perceiver. In the second, with an internal narrative of the listener or spectator, who is free to construct their own narrative inside the situation proposed by the author. External narrative inevitably deprives the internal narrative of the possibility of being born and significantly reduces the creative demand placed upon perception.

Music has another property: it unfolds in time. Music is heard time. Time in which we find ourselves alone with ourselves, even when surrounded by sounds. Are we ready to remain alone with ourselves long enough — for the duration of a concert? Or do we soon begin losing concentration and become bored? Does what is heard make us lose interest in listening, or do our listening skills prevent us from remaining in what is heard for a long time?

John Cage said that boredom is not outside us; boredom is inside us. Sit in silence and stillness, alone with yourself, for at least an hour. Listen to yourself, listen to how you react to time, to yourself in time, to how time lives within you. Discover yourself in time, or time in yourself. Stop time.

There is a territory on which the linear flow of time is abolished: memory. Here time is abolished altogether — everything is present simultaneously, and we freely pick out any memories regardless of their actual sequence. A traveler stops and focuses attention on individual events or objects, assembling them into an individual whole. Events are placed in the archive of memory like objects placed in space.
If we accept this scheme of relating to time, time becomes an attribute of perception, a consequence of the inability of human perception to encompass simultaneity, the eternal present.

If everything is present simultaneously, how can we imagine or comprehend the course of a musical or any other process unfolding sequentially and directionally, with a beginning and an end? Perhaps the process itself must be understood as an object situated in a space we conventionally call time — in the space of time. A writing desk, the process of making it from conception to realization, and Beethoven's Ninth Symphony composed at that desk are equally objects simultaneously situated, present, in space-time and comprehended by us in time as an attribute of our perception.
By 'stopping time', and with it stopping sound, we gain the possibility of looking inside it.

Listen closely to the environment around you, wherever you are: outdoors or indoors, in a noisy place or a quiet one, alone or in a crowd. Try to distinguish details — nearby or distant sounds, human voices or sounds of nature. Feel the depth and volume of audible space, change the focus of your hearing, move freely through it. Imagine that you are listening to a musical work that you are writing with your own hearing.

These practices change the paradigm of listening attention: from horizontal tracking of changing events we turn toward listening into the perspective of an event, discerning its properties and particularities.

New music offers not new sounds but new angles of listening. Yet this experience applies not only to the new: familiar classics can open before us from an unexpected angle, becoming no less new than something encountered for the first time. Ultimately, we are dealing not with sounds external to us, observed from a safe distance, but with how those sounds live within us, become us — that is, with ourselves.
If we learn to hear, to discover ourselves in listening, we will inevitably hear music as well. Music can be heard only by letting it into oneself, by becoming it.

To begin understanding the context and details, one needs to listen a great deal and for long periods, read about authors and works, styles and epochs, the nature of hearing and acoustics. But we should try not to displace our own internal narrative with an imposed external one. In acquiring knowledge, we must not lose ourselves or allow knowledge to replace us.

documents.title: To Be or Not to Be
paragraphs: All the texts in this series, while seemingly declaring the totality of loneliness, appear to deny the possibility of the existence of the Other and therefore the possibility of communication.

Indeed, I suspect that communication functions in one direction. By and large, we communicate like bats: we send a signal into emptiness, and by how quickly and how distorted it returns to us — if it returns at all — we judge the 'external world'. Ernst von Glasersfeld offers a metaphor very close to me: a person learns about the external world as a blind person learns about the forest through which they walk — from bruises and scratches. Radical constructivism says that the process of knowing reality is the process of constructing it.

Yet one of the principal driving forces of knowledge, and consequently of creativity, is doubt. Asking 'what am I?', we confront the eternal 'to be or not to be?' — defining our position in relation to what we allow ourselves to recognize as ourselves and what we do not. I see only one possible answer to this question: to doubt. It is not a question of choice; it is a rhetorical question. Somewhere between 'to be' and 'not to be' lies the doubting I.

At the same time, non-being is one of the states of being. 'To be' and 'not to be' are like inhalation and exhalation; it does not matter which is which, since each is simultaneously both and they condition one another, outlining the field of our existential and creative oscillations. Between inhalation and exhalation, between me and me, there is a space separating one from the other while itself being something third, a mysterious comma — the difference between one and the same. This difference is doubt.

The necessity of a creative act is born from doubt, from a sense of the insufficiency of what exists — more precisely, of its incomplete manifestation. This is not disappointment in what is present, nor its negation. It is constructive doubt. A creative person is a doubting person, carrying their own opinion — co-opinion.

Doubt expands knowledge. Every new text, including a musical one, is a chip or indentation in an a priori sum of texts, a potential of texts existing independently of our will. Through such indentations we learn about this sum, as scientists learn the properties of matter from a small fragment under a microscope. A new composition does not increase this sum; it expands our conception of it. It is already contained within that sum.

The self-referential, autopoietic world revealed before us — within us — with its closed communicative connections nevertheless does not deny the possibility of the Other: an Other existing, thinking, knowing, and creating in parallel. Not in dialogue, but in dilogue, polylogue — a sum of monologues unfolding each in its own dimension.

Thus the Other manifests itself through its absence. Like a Japanese rock garden arranged so that from every viewpoint one stone is always hidden behind the others. It is precisely this 'absent' stone that becomes the purpose and content of the art of arranging the garden.
